---
title: How sources are read
description: How Frame Job reads each kind of video and photo you bring in, and what it converts in an SDR project and in an HDR (HLG) project.
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Frame Job reads each source as what it is: ordinary video, HLG video, an HDR10 file, wide-gamut footage or camera log. You don't need to set anything for most footage, because the file's own colour labels say how to read it. The one kind you may have to name yourself is camera log.

<AtAGlance
  menu={['File ▸ Add Media…', 'View ▸ Show Ungraded']}
  keys={['⇧⌘I', '⌃⌘U']}
  where={['Media tab ▸ Camera Log', 'Media tab ▸ HDR10']}
  tools={['import_media', 'set_media_color']}
/>

## One conversion at the start

Each frame of a source is converted once, before anything else happens to it, into the colour the project works in. That's Rec. 709 in an SDR project and Rec. 2100 HLG over BT.2020 in an HDR (HLG) project. See [A project's dynamic range](/hdr/dynamic-range/) for how to choose.

The chroma key and every grade then see the converted picture, so they work the same whatever the file was. The file's labels choose the conversion, and a [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/) set on the file chooses before its labels. The conversion is Frame Job's own, for HLG, PQ and wide-gamut sources alike.

An SDR project that holds only Rec. 709 sources isn't converted at all. Its pixels and labels stay exactly as they are, because Frame Job turns the conversion on only when a source needs it.

A few terms come up below. A file's **primaries** say which colours its red, green and blue are, and its **transfer curve** says how its numbers turn into brightness. Brightness is measured in cd/m². A highlight that's **rolled off** is eased down to the brightest level the picture can show, rather than cut off flat.

| Source | In an SDR project | In an HDR (HLG) project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Rec. 709 or untagged](#rec-709-and-untagged-sources) | Drawn as it is | Lifted to HDR reference white, so it looks the same |
| [HLG video](#hlg-video) | Converted to Rec. 709, highlights rolled off smoothly | Kept as HLG, highlights above white intact |
| [PQ or HDR10 video](#pq-and-hdr10-video) | Converted to Rec. 709, highlights rolled off at the file's own peak | Real HDR, up to 1,000 cd/m² |
| [Wide-gamut SDR](#wide-gamut-sdr) | Converted to Rec. 709 | Converted into BT.2020 and lifted |
| [Camera log](#camera-log) | Converted to a normal-looking Rec. 709 picture | Converted to real HDR |
| [HLG or PQ still](#hdr-stills) | Converted as a video of the same kind is | Drawn in its own colour, as HDR |
| [Gain-map photo](#gain-map-photos) | Its ordinary picture | Its HDR highlights |

## Rec. 709 and untagged sources

Ordinary Rec. 709 video, video with no colour labels, recordings and stills are drawn as they are in an SDR project.

In an HDR (HLG) project they're lifted to HDR reference white, the level ordinary white sits at: 203 cd/m², or 75 % of the HLG signal. They look the same as they do in SDR, and HDR highlights rise above them. Text, captions, shapes, graphics and the background colour are lifted the same way.

## HLG video

HLG video, such as iPhone HDR video, needs no setting. The file's own colour labels choose the conversion.

- **In an SDR project** it's converted to Rec. 709 with its highlights rolled off smoothly. A colour Rec. 709 can't show is eased toward its own brightness instead of being clipped.
- **In an HDR (HLG) project** it stays HLG, with its highlights above white intact. An HLG file over BT.2020 is used exactly as it is, and one over P3 or BT.709 primaries is converted into BT.2020.

In an SDR project, HLG is converted whatever its primaries. A file whose primaries are absent or unknown is read as BT.2020.

## PQ and HDR10 video

A PQ file, usually called HDR10, is always converted.

- **In an SDR project** its highlights roll off to white at the peak read from the file. Colours outside Rec. 709 are eased toward their brightness, as with HLG. You can override the peak in the Media tab's **HDR10** section. See [HDR10 peak](/hdr/hdr10-peak/).
- **In an HDR (HLG) project** it becomes real HDR, keeping its brightness up to 1,000 cd/m². If the file's peak is above that, its highlights are rolled off to fit. A peak of 1,000 cd/m² or less doesn't change the picture.

A file whose primaries are absent or unknown is read as BT.2020, as with HLG.

## Wide-gamut SDR

A source with BT.2020 or P3 D65 primaries and an SDR transfer curve, sRGB included, is converted to the project's colours rather than drawn with the wrong ones. This happens by itself, from the file's labels.

- **In an SDR project** it's converted to Rec. 709. Colours Rec. 709 can't show are clipped.
- **In an HDR (HLG) project** it's converted into BT.2020 and lifted, so those colours survive.

An SDR project always works in Rec. 709. To keep a wide-gamut source's colours, use an HDR (HLG) project.

## sRGB-transfer files

A source labelled with the sRGB transfer curve is read as sRGB rather than as Rec. 709. This is automatic too. Primaries that are absent or unrecognised read as BT.709.

An sRGB file with BT.709 primaries never turns the conversion on by itself. It's read as sRGB when something else in the project needs converting, and it looks the same either way. With BT.2020 or P3 D65 primaries it counts as [wide-gamut SDR](#wide-gamut-sdr).

## Full-range files

A file stores its levels in video range, a narrower band of the available codes, or in full range, all of them. S-Log3 and V-Log files can be stored either way, and the two need reading differently. Frame Job takes the range from the file's full-range flag. If a VP9 video has no flag, it reads the range from the VP9 track's own settings. A file with neither is read as video range.

Apple Log, Apple Log 2, C-Log2 and C-Log3 are read the same way whatever the flag says.

:::caution
A non-ProRes Canon file flagged as video range that actually stores full-range codes looks too contrasty after C-Log2 or C-Log3 conversion.
:::

## Camera log

Log footage looks flat and grey until it's converted, and this is the one kind of source you may have to name. Frame Job recognises Apple Log and Apple Log 2 by themselves. For Sony, Panasonic and Canon footage, choose the curve in the Media tab's **Camera Log** section. See [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/).

- **In an SDR project** the footage becomes a normal-looking Rec. 709 picture.
- **In an HDR (HLG) project** it's converted to HLG instead of Rec. 709, with no highlight roll-off, so it's real HDR.

## HDR stills

A still labelled HLG or PQ is treated as HDR, the way a video of the same kind is, rather than being read as SDR. Bring it in with **File ▸ Add Media…** (<kbd>⇧⌘I</kbd>) as you would any picture. This works for PNG and HEIC, which keep their colour space and depth.

- **In an SDR project** the still converts as an HLG or PQ video does.
- **In an HDR (HLG) project** it's drawn in its own colour, as HDR.

Display P3, BT.709 and BT.2020 primaries are recognised, and any other reads as BT.2020.

A PQ still has an [HDR10 peak](/hdr/hdr10-peak/) like a PQ video. It takes a peak but no Camera Log.

A still deeper than 8 bits per channel that isn't labelled HDR is an ordinary SDR picture, drawn at full depth. See [Precision and bit depth](/hdr/precision/).

## Gain-map photos

An iPhone HDR photo is a HEIC with a gain map: an ordinary picture plus the information to brighten its highlights. Frame Job reads ISO 21496-1 and Apple HDR gain maps.

- **In an HDR (HLG) project** the photo shows its HDR highlights.
- **In an SDR project, and in every thumbnail,** it shows its ordinary picture.

In the SDR version of an HDR project, the photo is its HDR rendition toned down, not the photo's own SDR image. That covers [Show SDR Version](/hdr/show-sdr-version/), JPEG frames and SDR-version exports.

A chroma key picked on a gain-map photo keys close to, but not exactly, what it keyed before a switch to HDR (HLG). Re-pick the key if an edge changes.

## The same everywhere

The conversion works the same way in the preview, in every export, and in rendered and saved frames.

The timeline's filmstrip and the Media tab's thumbnails follow it too:

- Filmstrips of log, PQ and HLG files show the converted picture, not the raw file. In an SDR project that's the picture in the preview. In an HDR (HLG) project they're drawn as an SDR project would draw them.
- An HLG or PQ still's thumbnail is drawn the same way. It appears a moment after import, once it's been converted.
- Changing a PQ file's peak redraws its strip, as changing a file's Camera Log does.

**View ▸ Show Ungraded** (<kbd>⌃⌘U</kbd>) turns off the grades but leaves this conversion on, because the conversion is how the file is read, not part of the grade. See [Show Ungraded](/color/show-ungraded/).

## Good to know

- Camera Log and the HDR10 peak belong to the file, not to a clip, so two clips of one file can't be read differently.
- HDR reference white is fixed at 203 cd/m². There's no setting for it.
- A chroma key on HLG footage with P3 or BT.709 primaries, or on PQ highlights above 1,000 cd/m², is close but not exact after a switch to HDR (HLG). [A project's dynamic range](/hdr/dynamic-range/) has the detail.

## Related

- [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/)
- [HDR10 peak](/hdr/hdr10-peak/)
- [A project's dynamic range](/hdr/dynamic-range/)
- [Show Ungraded](/color/show-ungraded/)
- [Import media](/projects/import-media/)
---
title: Camera Log
description: Tell Frame Job which log curve a video file was shot with, so flat footage looks right in the preview, the grade and every export.
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

Log footage looks flat and grey until it's converted. Camera Log tells Frame Job which curve a video file was shot with, so the file displays as a normal picture before you grade it.

<AtAGlance
  where="Media tab ▸ Camera Log ▸ Log"
  tools={['set_media_color', 'get_project', 'import_media', 'undo']}
  needs="A video file in the project."
/>

## Set a file's Camera Log

The **Camera Log** section appears in the Media tab once the project has a video file.

<Steps>

1. Open the **Media** tab in the inspector.

2. Click the file in the list.

3. Choose the curve from the **Log** popup. Pick the row that matches how the camera was set.

</Steps>

<Shot
  name="10b-media-tab.inspector"
  alt="The Media tab with three files listed. Below the list, the Camera Log section has a Log popup reading None, dimmed, with the line Select a video in the list under it, because no video row is selected yet."
/>

Apple Log and Apple Log 2 files are [set for you on import](#detection-on-import). Sony, Panasonic and Canon files have to be set by hand.

## The Log popup

| Item | Curve | Camera gamut |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **None** | No conversion: the file shows its log picture as recorded | |
| **Apple Log** | Apple Log | BT.2020 |
| **Apple Log 2** | Apple Log | Apple Wide Gamut |
| **S-Log3 / S-Gamut3.Cine** | Sony S-Log3 | S-Gamut3.Cine |
| **S-Log3 / S-Gamut3** | Sony S-Log3 | S-Gamut3 |
| **V-Log / V-Gamut** | Panasonic V-Log | V-Gamut |
| **C-Log2 / Cinema Gamut** | Canon Log 2 | Cinema Gamut |
| **C-Log2 / BT.2020** | Canon Log 2 | BT.2020 |
| **C-Log3 / Cinema Gamut** | Canon Log 3 | Cinema Gamut |
| **C-Log3 / BT.2020** | Canon Log 3 | BT.2020 |

Below these, the popup lists **LUT:** and the name of each `.cube` LUT in the project, then **Use LUT…**. A file is converted by a maker's curve or by a LUT, never both. See [Camera log from your own LUT](/hdr/log-luts/).

Choosing **None** on a PQ file keeps its [HDR10 peak](/hdr/hdr10-peak/) override. It's also how you see the raw log picture of a file Frame Job set by itself.

:::caution
A non-ProRes Canon file flagged as video range that actually stores full-range codes looks too contrasty after C-Log2 or C-Log3 conversion. See [Full-range files](/hdr/how-sources-are-read/#full-range-files).
:::

## A setting on the file

Camera Log belongs to the media file, not to a clip. Every clip of the file follows it, reversed clips included, and two clips of one file can't be read differently. The HDR10 peak belongs to the file in the same way, and changing one keeps the other.

Relinking a file with **Relink…** keeps its Camera Log.

Each change is one undo step, named **Camera Log**. Picking the row that's already showing changes nothing and makes no undo step.

## What the section says

A line under the popup says what's set. The section's header repeats the selected file's curve or LUT name, so you can read it with the section closed.

| The line reads | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| The setting, such as "S-Log3 / S-Gamut3.Cine" or "LUT: name" | You chose this row. |
| The setting with "— from the file", such as "Apple Log — from the file" | Frame Job read it from the file's label on import. |
| "None" | Nothing is set, so the file shows as recorded. |
| "Select a video in the list" | The selected row isn't a video file, or no row is selected. The popup is disabled. |

## Detection on import

An Apple Log or Apple Log 2 file is recognised by its label when you import it, so it looks like normal video straight away. Apple Log is paired with BT.2020 and Apple Log 2 with Apple Wide Gamut, and the line under the popup adds "— from the file".

To see the raw log picture of such a file, choose **None**. If you then choose its curve again by hand, the line no longer says "— from the file".

Only the two Apple curves are detected. Sony, Panasonic and Canon files carry no label Frame Job can read, so choose S-Log3, V-Log, C-Log2 or C-Log3 yourself.

## How a curve is displayed

Each built-in curve follows its maker's published curve and gamut. Cinema Gamut's primaries come from the ACES project's Canon transform. Frame Job's display transform then turns the footage into a normal-looking picture.

The table shows where a grey card's 18 % and a white card's 90 % land, as signal levels from 0 % at black to 100 % at the top of the scale.

| | In an SDR project | In an HDR (HLG) project |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 18 % grey | 42 % | HLG 38 % |
| 90 % white | About 78 % | Not rolled off |
| Highlights | Roll off smoothly up to about six stops over grey | Real HDR, with no roll-off |

## Thumbnails follow

Changing a file's Camera Log redraws its thumbnails in the Media tab and its filmstrip on the timeline, so they show the converted picture. In an HDR (HLG) project they show it as an SDR project would draw it.

## Before the grade

The conversion happens before the chroma key and before every grade step. It comes ahead of every step of the [grade order](/color/color-tab/#the-fixed-grade-order), Color, Light, Wheels, Curves and Look, so a grade works on the converted picture, not on flat log. **View ▸ Show Ungraded** (<kbd>⌃⌘U</kbd>) keeps it on, because it's how the file is read.

If a clip's file has a Camera Log and you also give the clip a LUT as a [look](/color/luts/), the Look section warns: "This clip's file is converted by Camera Log; a camera LUT here converts it twice." It's only a warning, because a creative LUT on top is fine.

## Which files it works on

Camera Log is for video files only. It can't go on an audio file, an image or a LUT, and the popup is disabled for those rows. A PQ still takes an [HDR10 peak](/hdr/hdr10-peak/) but no Camera Log.

## With an agent

`set_media_color` sets or clears a file's Camera Log. `get_project` reads it back in `media[].color`, with `detected: true` for a file Frame Job set on import. [Tools: media](/mcp/tools-media/#set_media_color) has the value for each curve and gamut.

An agent differs from the popup in these ways:

- Clearing a file's Camera Log from an agent also clears a PQ file's peak override, where **None** keeps it. To keep the override, an agent sends it along with the new setting.
- The call fails, with a message saying why, if it pairs a curve with a gamut that curve doesn't take, gives a gamut with no curve, gives a curve and a LUT together, or names a LUT that isn't in the project. The popup never offers those.
- An agent can't set `detected` or the file's own peak reading in `pq`. Only import writes them.
- The call also fails if it names a nest in its `scope` argument, because Camera Log belongs to the file. With a nest open through `set_scope`, the call still reaches the file, as the popup does.

## Related

---
title: "Camera log from your own LUT"
description: "Convert a log file with a .cube LUT instead of a built-in curve, share that LUT between files, and remove it without surprises."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

Log footage looks flat until it's converted. When [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/) has no built-in curve for your footage, a `.cube` LUT, a file that maps one set of colours to another, can do the conversion instead. You pick the LUT once, and every clip of that file comes out as normal-looking video.

<AtAGlance
  where={['Media tab ▸ Camera Log ▸ Log ▸ Use LUT…', 'Media tab ▸ Camera Log ▸ Log ▸ LUT: name']}
  tools={['import_media', 'set_media_color', 'remove_media']}
/>

## Use LUT…

<Steps>

1. Open the **Media** tab and click the video file in the list.

2. In the **Camera Log** section, choose **Use LUT…** from the **Log** popup.

3. Pick the `.cube` file. The panel asks you to "Choose a .cube LUT that converts this file's log footage to Rec. 709."

</Steps>

The LUT joins the project's media list and becomes this file's conversion, all as one undo step called **Camera Log**. The line under the popup and the section's header then read **LUT: name**.

Frame Job takes the LUT's output as Rec. 709, so use a LUT made for that job. Like every Camera Log setting, it belongs to the file: every clip of the file follows it, reversed clips included, and it's applied before the chroma key and every grade.

A file takes a curve or a LUT, not both, so choosing one replaces the other. A PQ file keeps its [peak override](/hdr/hdr10-peak/#undo-and-camera-log).

If the file you pick is already in the Media list, Frame Job uses that entry and doesn't add a second one.

The LUT has to be a 3D `.cube` of size 2 to 65 with the default 0 to 1 domain, and no larger than 32 MiB. Anything else shows an error naming the file and what's wrong with it, and nothing changes. For example: "“Film.cube” is not a LUT Frame Job reads: line 2: LUT_3D_SIZE 200 is outside 2–65." [.cube LUTs](/color/luts/) has the format in full.

## A LUT already in the project

Every `.cube` LUT in the project is listed in the **Log** popup as **LUT: name**, between the built-in curves and **Use LUT…**. The name is the file's name without `.cube`.

To use the same LUT on another file, click that file in the list and choose its row. One LUT can convert any number of files.

The popup and the [Look section](/color/looks/) read the same media list. A LUT you imported as a look is offered here, and a LUT you added with **Use LUT…** appears in the Look section's Imported group.

To take a LUT off one file, choose **None** or a curve in the **Log** popup. The LUT stays in the Media list.

## A LUT in use

A LUT that is some file's Camera Log counts as used, even when no clip has it as a look. **Unused only** hides it from the [Media list](/projects/media-tab/#unused-only), and **Remove** asks before it takes the LUT away.

## Remove the LUT

Right-click the LUT's row on the Media tab and choose **Remove**. The alert says what depends on it, for example:

- "It is the Camera Log of 2 files, which lose it."
- "It is the look of 1 clip, which keeps its place and loses the look. …and the Camera Log of 2 files, which lose it."

**Remove and Clear Looks** removes the LUT as one undo step, **Remove Media**. Those files go back to no conversion, so they show the log picture as recorded. Clips that had it as a look stay where they are and lose the look. A PQ file keeps its peak. **Cancel** changes nothing.

The `.cube` file on your disk is never touched. See [Remove media](/projects/remove-media/).

## Camera Log and looks

Camera Log is applied before any look, so a look works on the picture the conversion made.

If a clip's look is a `.cube` LUT and its file has a Camera Log, the Look section warns: "This clip's file is converted by Camera Log; a camera LUT here converts it twice."

It's only a warning, and Frame Job changes nothing, because a creative LUT on top of a conversion is fine. If the look really is a camera LUT, keep it in one place: either in the **Log** popup or as the clip's look, not both.

The eight built-in looks never show this warning. A `.cube` look on a PQ (HDR10) file does show it, even with **Log** set to **None**.

## Good to know

- In an HDR (HLG) project, a LUT's output is treated as SDR and [lifted to reference white](/hdr/dynamic-range/#sdr-material-in-an-hdr-project), so the file gains no HDR highlights. A built-in curve does become real HDR there.
- If the LUT can't be found or drawn, the footage shows unconverted, as flat log, until you [relink](/projects/relink-media/) the LUT. A LUT relinks like any other file in the Media list.
- Relinking the video file keeps its Camera Log.
- Camera Log is for video files. With an audio file, an image or a LUT selected, the popup is disabled and the line reads "Select a video in the list".
- **View ▸ Show Ungraded** turns looks and grades off and leaves the conversion on, because the conversion is how the file is read.

## With an agent

An agent takes two steps where a person takes one: `import_media` brings the `.cube` into the project, then [`set_media_color`](/mcp/tools-media/#set_media_color) names it as the file's conversion, with `color` set to `{lut: <media id>}`. The call can't set a curve and a LUT together.

`remove_media` won't take a LUT that's in use unless the call passes `with_clips: true`, which clears the conversions and looks that name it. See [Tools: media](/mcp/tools-media/#remove_media).

---
title: "HDR10 peak"
description: "See the peak brightness Frame Job read from a PQ file, override it when the metadata is wrong or missing, and go back to the file's own value."
---

import { Steps } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';
import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';

HDR10 video uses the PQ transfer curve, so Frame Job calls it a PQ file. Such a file's metadata names how bright its highlights get, and Frame Job eases them down to white at that brightness, its peak, rather than cutting them off flat. The peak is read when you import the file, and the **HDR10** section lets you see it and change it when the metadata is wrong or missing.

<AtAGlance
  where="Media tab ▸ HDR10"
  tools={['set_media_color', 'get_project']}
/>

## The peak a file names

Import reads the peak by itself, so most files need nothing from you. It takes MaxCLL, the brightest pixel the file says it holds, when that's present and not zero. Otherwise it takes the maximum of the display the file was mastered on.

| The file is | Frame Job looks in |
| --- | --- |
| A video | The description stored with the video track. When that carries no HDR10 metadata at all, the video stream's own (HEVC SEI or AV1 metadata), so files from ffmpeg, HandBrake or x265 are read too. |
| A PNG still | Its `cLLI` and `mDCV` chunks. |
| A HEIF or HEIC still | The `clli` and `mdcv` boxes of its main image. |

A file that names no peak is still read as PQ, and it's treated as 1,000 cd/m².

What the peak does depends on the [project's dynamic range](/hdr/dynamic-range/):

- **In an SDR project**, highlights roll off smoothly to white at the peak. A peak below 203 cd/m², HDR reference white (the level ordinary white sits at), counts as 203.
- **In an HDR (HLG) project**, the picture keeps display light up to 1,000 cd/m². A peak above that rolls brighter highlights off to fit, and a lower peak doesn't change the picture.

## The HDR10 section

The **HDR10** section of the **Media** tab appears once the project has a PQ file, either a video or a still.

Click the file in the list to see and change its peak. The section's header shows the selected file's peak, for example "4,000 cd/m²", so you can read it with the section closed.

When the selected row isn't a PQ file, the section reads "Select a PQ file in the list" and its controls are disabled.

## Set a peak by hand

Override the file's peak when its metadata is wrong, or when it has none and you know the real figure.

<Steps>

1. On the **Media** tab, click the PQ file in the list.

2. In the **HDR10** section, type a value in **Peak** and press <kbd>↩</kbd>, or click the chevron for a [quick pick](/getting-started/inspector-fields/#use-a-quick-pick).

</Steps>

**Peak** takes whole numbers from 1 to 10,000 cd/m², and its quick picks are 1,000, 2,000, 4,000 and 10,000. A typed number outside the range is held to the nearest end. Entering the value already showing isn't a new choice, so it makes no undo step.

## Use File's

**Use File's** clears your override and goes back to the peak the file's HDR10 metadata names. A file with no metadata goes back to the assumed 1,000 cd/m².

The button is available only while an override is set.

## Where the peak came from

A line under the controls says where the peak came from.

| The line says | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| "Mastered at 4,000 cd/m² (MaxCLL, from the file)" | The file's own value. |
| "No HDR10 metadata — 1,000 cd/m² assumed" | The file names no peak. |
| "Set by hand; the file says 1,000 cd/m² (mastering display)" | Your override, with the value it replaces. |
| "Set by hand; the file has no HDR10 metadata" | Your override, on a file with no metadata. |

## Undo and Camera Log

Each change is one undo step, **PQ Peak**.

The peak and the [Camera Log](/hdr/camera-log/) keep each other. Changing the peak keeps the file's Camera Log setting, and changing the Camera Log, even to **None**, keeps the peak.

## Good to know

- The peak belongs to the media file, not to a clip, so two clips of one file can't be read differently.
- Only a PQ file has a peak, so the section's controls are disabled for anything else.
- The peak is read once, at import. Relinking a PQ file doesn't read it again, so set it by hand if the new file differs. A file that wasn't PQ when you imported it can't take a peak after you relink it to one.
- A PQ still takes a peak and nothing else. Camera Log is for video files.
- The peak describes a source file. An [HDR10 export](/hdr/export-hdr/) carries fixed metadata of its own, whatever the peak is.

## With an agent

`set_media_color` sets a PQ file's peak with `peak` in its `color`, a whole number of cd/m². A PQ still takes `peak` alone. `get_project` shows the file's own reading in `media[].color.pq`, where an empty `{}` means the file names no peak.

Two things differ from the app:

- The call replaces the Camera Log and the peak together, so an agent that wants to keep both sends both. In the app each control keeps the other.
- `color: null` clears the Camera Log and a peak override together, and the peak goes back to the file's own reading.

The call fails in two cases where the app can't go wrong:

| The agent sends | What comes back |
| --- | --- |
| A peak outside 1 to 10,000, which the field would hold to the range | "color.peak must be 1–10000 cd/m², not …" |
| A peak on a file that isn't PQ | "media N is not a PQ file; only a PQ file takes a peak" |

See [Tools: media](/mcp/tools-media/#set_media_color).

- [A project's dynamic range](/hdr/dynamic-range/)
- [Relink missing media](/projects/relink-media/)

title: "Scopes"
description: "Open the Scopes panel beside the preview to measure the picture while you grade, with two slots that each show a waveform, parade, vectorscope or histogram."
---

import AtAGlance from '@components/AtAGlance.astro';
import Shot from '@components/Shot.astro';

Scopes measure the picture while you grade, so you're not relying on your eyes or your display. The panel sits beside the preview and shows two scopes at once.

<AtAGlance menu="View ▸ Scopes" keys="⌃⌘W" tools="render_frame" />

<Shot
  name="04b-preview-scopes.preview"
  alt="The preview with the Scopes panel on its right. The top slot shows a Waveform with red clip marks and the readouts Highlights clipped 1.9 % and Shadows clipped 52.7 %. The bottom slot shows a Vectorscope with its six colour targets and 1×, 2× and 4× zoom cells. Both slots are captioned Rec. 709 · encoded."
/>

## Open the scopes

Press <kbd>⌃⌘W</kbd>, or choose **View ▸ Scopes**. Do the same again to close the panel. The menu item has a checkmark while it's open, and it's always available.

The panel is a fixed column 248 pt wide, the full height of the preview pane, between the picture and the inspector. The picture shrinks to fit what's left, and takes the whole pane back when the panel closes. If the [Loudness Meter](/audio/loudness-meter/) is on too, its column sits between the picture and the scopes.

The panel is off in every new window. Your scope choices and zooms last while the window is open, even if you close and reopen the panel, and they aren't saved.

## Choose a scope for each slot

The panel has two slots, one above the other. Each has a popup at its top left that picks one of four scopes. A new window opens on **Waveform** over **Vectorscope**.

| Scope | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| [Waveform](/color/waveform-and-parade/#read-the-waveform) | Brightness across the frame, left to right. |
| [Parade](/color/waveform-and-parade/#read-the-rgb-parade) | Red, green and blue as three waveforms side by side. |
| [Vectorscope](/color/vectorscope/) | Hue and saturation, with colour targets and the skin line. |
| [Histogram](/color/histogram/) | How many pixels sit at each level, per colour. |

You can put the same scope in both slots. Each slot keeps its own vectorscope zoom, so two vectorscopes can show the picture at different zooms.

## Read a slot's caption

A faint caption at each slot's top right says what the scope is reading.

| Project | Waveform and Parade | Vectorscope and Histogram |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SDR | Rec. 709 · encoded | Rec. 709 · encoded |
| HDR (HLG) | HLG · cd/m² | Rec. 2100 HLG |

"Encoded" means the scope reads the picture's stored values, not the light they stand for. An HDR project also changes the scales and targets. See [Scopes in an HDR project](/hdr/hdr-scopes/).

40:Choose **Pick from Canvas** and the preview reads "Click to pick the key color · Esc to cancel". One click on the picture sets **Key Color**. The button works with the key off, and a pick turns it on.
54:Only one canvas tool is ready at a time. **Pick from Canvas** ends [Obscure](/effects/obscure/)'s **Place on Canvas**, [Zoom to Region](/motion/zoom-to-region/) and the [qualifier's Pick from Canvas](/color/pick-from-canvas/).
80:With an [action](/motion/edit-an-action/) selected, **Key Color**, **Tolerance**, **Softness** and **Spill** set the value at the action's end and animate toward it. The colour blends through the OKLab colour space along the action. **Pick from Canvas** also sends its colour to the action's end.
